title: Prime-Power Desert
statement: Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there are $n$ consecutive positive integers, none of which is a prime power. (A prime power is a number $p^k$ with $p$ prime and $k \ge 1$.)
hints: It is enough for each of the $n$ numbers to have two different prime factors.
Pick $2n$ distinct primes and use the Chinese remainder theorem.
solution: Choose distinct primes $p_1, q_1, \dots, p_n, q_n$. By the Chinese remainder theorem there is a positive integer $x$ with $x \equiv -i \pmod{p_i q_i}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$. Then $x + i$ is divisible by the two different primes $p_i$ and $q_i$, so it is not a prime power. The numbers $x+1, \dots, x+n$ work.

rubric.criterion: reducing to 'each number has two distinct prime factors'
checking every number in the block, with no gaps
